title: Ukraine’s defense tech sector must offer investors more than innovation
author: Peter Dickinson
text:
Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has built one of the world’s most dynamic defense technology ecosystems under conditions few industries ever face. Technologies can move from development to battlefield deployment within months or even weeks, receiving immediate feedback from the front lines. This unprecedented battlefield validation has emerged as one of Ukraine’s most distinctive features.

For international investors, this represents an unusual form of technological validation. Technologies tested against a sophisticated adversary under wartime conditions offer advantages that laboratory trials and peacetime exercises cannot easily replicate. Meanwhile, investment can bring Ukraine a range of potential benefits including additional budget revenues, improved research and development potential, expanded production lines, and economies of scale. However, innovation alone will not be enough to win over investors.

No other country in the democratic world can match the rapid battlefield validation that Ukrainian defense tech companies can currently provide, but this is only one of multiple features necessary to secure international investment. Defense industry participants consistently highlight the distinction between developing specific technologies and building a company capable of providing investors with the long-term returns they are seeking.

Investment decisions relating to the Ukrainian defense tech sector are based primarily on a sober assessment of the security and legislative environments. In other words, do the companies under consideration have credible strategies to remain in business amid extremely challenging wartime conditions, and is a reliable legal framework in place that will allow them to operate domestically and internationally? Key questions also include whether Ukrainian defense tech companies can manufacture at scale, manage larger contracts and work forces, maintain financial discipline, protect intellectual property, and comply with international regulations.

These requirements are already redefining the Ukrainian defense tech sector as a generation of new companies matures. Many of these companies were established in response to Russia’s full-scale invasion by groups of engineers, tech entrepreneurs, and military personnel, who came together to address urgent battlefield problems. Some have since expanded from small engineering teams to become substantial businesses. In many cases, corporate structures that would conventionally develop over much longer periods have had to evolve alongside extraordinary production growth.

As Ukrainian defense tech businesses scale, the nature of the investment risk also evolves. Early in a company’s development, the central question is whether the technology works. Once operational performance has been demonstrated, the focus shifts. Can the company reproduce current levels of performance consistently and absorb additional capital effectively? Are revenues, costs, ownership issues, and commercial pipelines sufficiently understood? Can the company expand beyond a single product or customer?

Even the term “battle-tested” requires closer scrutiny. Investors generally recognize that this can describe very different levels of operational validation, from limited front line trials to sustained deployment. They consequently look beyond the label and seek to assess depth and continuity of battlefield use, credible military-user feedback, procurement evidence where available, and continued access to the operational learning that allows a product to evolve.

The relentless cycle of innovation is a crucial factor shaping investment decisions. With new military technologies and upgrades reshaping the Ukrainian battlefield on a regular basis, a company’s competitive advantage depends less on the quality of current tech than on the ability to maintain a high level of innovative adaptation. From an investment perspective, the most valuable asset of all is not today’s product line but the supporting infrastructure of engineering capability, operational knowledge, and military feedback relationships that generate the next iteration.

The nature of the Ukrainian defense tech industry, which has emerged amid a major ongoing war, creates specific due diligence issues for investors. In many cases, Ukrainian defense manufacturers cannot freely disclose details of existing clients, production locations, battlefield data, or other technical information. While few would question the legitimacy of these restrictions, they do nevertheless serve as practical obstacles to investment. Solutions include limited disclosure to specified persons and qualified third-party review. These mechanisms can help investors make informed assessments without posing a security threat.

Ukraine already has a number of initiatives designed to enhance engagement between the country’s defense tech companies and potential international investors. Leading the way is Brave1, a state institution launched in spring 2023 that aims to serve as a defense tech cluster with a focus on bringing Ukrainian companies and investors together. As the market evolves, this infrastructure can increasingly address the financial, legal, governance, IP, and verification requirements of larger strategic and institutional transactions.

If Ukrainian defense tech companies wish to continue growing, they will need to adapt. There are signs that market consolidation is already well underway, while the next round of international investment is likely to be far larger than the initial stages. While specialist investors familiar with Ukraine can accept levels of geopolitical, technological, and informational uncertainty, this is unlikely to be the case for banks, strategic investors, and institutions. In order to attract capital, ambitious Ukrainian companies must address investor expectations without undermining the speed and innovation that have made the country’s defense tech sector so attractive.

Olga Usenko is a former visiting fellow at the Atlantic Council’s Eurasia Center.
